title: Sudoku Solver
description: Brute force to optimized: validating a full board only at the end versus backtracking with row/column/box checks before every placement.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a partially filled 9 by 9 Sudoku board, with empty cells marked ".", fill in the empty cells so that each row, each column, and each of the nine 3 by 3 sub-boxes contains every digit from 1 to 9 exactly once. It is guaranteed the puzzle has exactly one solution.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Every empty cell must be filled with a digit from 1 to 9 such that no row, column, or 3x3 box ends up with a repeated digit. Since the puzzle is guaranteed to have exactly one solution, a systematic search that tries digits and backtracks on failure will always find it.

blocks.title: Analogy: Filling in a Seating Chart with Three Overlapping Rules
blocks.text: Picture assigning people to seats in a 9x9 grid where no two people in the same row, same column, or same 3x3 section of the room can share the same assigned role. This problem is exactly that: fill every empty seat so all three overlapping constraints hold everywhere.

blocks.caption: A digit is valid at a cell only if it is absent from that row, that column, AND that 3x3 box

blocks.text: Given the well-known example puzzle, the unique solution fills every "." with the digit that satisfies all three constraints simultaneously, ultimately producing a fully valid, completed board.

Before trying every possible full-board digit assignment, notice that filling cells one at a time, left to right, top to bottom, and checking a digit's validity against its row/column/box BEFORE placing it, prunes invalid branches the moment they arise, the same backtracking-with-pruning idea used in N-Queens.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Scanning the board in a fixed order (row by row, left to right) and finding the next empty cell gives a deterministic order to attempt placements in.

Observation 2: For the current empty cell, trying digits 1 through 9 and checking each against the cell's row, column, and 3x3 box BEFORE placing it means only genuinely valid placements are ever attempted, avoiding wasted exploration.

Observation 3: After placing a valid digit, recursing to solve the rest of the board (starting the search for the next empty cell) either succeeds (in which case the whole board is done) or fails, in which case the digit must be removed (backtracked) and the next candidate digit tried.

Observation 4: The base case is finding no more empty cells, meaning the board is completely and validly filled.

This leads to scanning for the next empty cell, trying digits 1-9 with a row/column/box validity check before placing each, recursing on success, and backtracking (removing the digit) on failure to try the next candidate.

A more literal brute force would try every possible digit assignment for every empty cell independently, only validating the ENTIRE board once every cell has some digit, rather than checking validity as each digit is placed.

items: Enumerate every combination of digit assignments to the empty cells.
For each complete assignment, check every row, column, and 3x3 box for validity.
Keep the first (and, by the problem's guarantee, only) fully valid assignment.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Validating only after the whole board is filled means countless invalid partial assignments are fully completed before being discarded.
This is correct in principle but computationally infeasible for anything beyond a near-empty board.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: up to O(9^m) where m is the number of empty cells, with no pruning until a full board is built.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the board itself.

Limitation: validating only at the very end wastes enormous effort on partial assignments that are already invalid; checking row/column/box validity BEFORE placing each digit prunes these branches immediately.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking validity only at the end is wasteful: most partial digit placements will conflict with an earlier placement in the same row, column, or box; discovering this only after the whole board is filled means countless invalid combinations get fully explored.

The fix, exactly as in N-Queens: check a candidate digit's validity against its row, column, and box IMMEDIATELY, before placing it, so invalid digits are never even tried further.

How recursion proceeds: find the next empty cell (scanning row by row); for each digit 1-9 valid at that cell, place it, recurse to solve the rest of the board, and if the recursive call succeeds, the whole board is done; otherwise, remove the digit (backtrack) and try the next candidate.

The core idea: place digits one empty cell at a time, checking all three constraint types before each placement, and backtrack on failure.

Scan for the next empty cell. Try digits 1-9, checking row/column/box validity before placing. Recurse into the rest of the board; if the recursive attempt fails, undo the placement and try the next digit.
Result on the classic example puzzle

blocks.caption: Find the next empty cell, try valid digits, recurse, backtrack (undo) on failure

blocks.text: Checking row, column, and box validity BEFORE placing each digit guarantees every partial board explored during the search is always valid so far. This means the recursion never wastes effort completing an assignment doomed to fail; any conflict is caught the instant it would occur, and the search backtracks immediately to try the next digit or the previous cell.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: bounded by O(9^m) in the worst theoretical case (m empty cells), but heavily pruned in practice, solving typical puzzles almost instantly.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the board (recursion depth bounded by the number of empty cells).

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "this generalizes N-Queens's row-by-row, immediate-pruning backtracking to three overlapping constraint types (row, column, box)" ties the technique to a well-known pattern the interviewer will recognize.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "fill cells satisfying multiple overlapping constraints", think: backtrack cell by cell, validate all constraint types BEFORE placing, undo on failure.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The unpruned brute force is computationally infeasible for non-trivial puzzles; the backtracking approach with immediate constraint checks is fast in practice due to heavy pruning, despite a theoretical worst case.

items: Pattern: constraint-satisfaction backtracking, filling cells one at a time with validity checks before each placement.
Core Idea: find the next empty cell, try each digit 1-9 valid against its row/column/box, recurse, and undo on failure.
Time: up to O(9^m) unpruned, heavily pruned and fast in practice for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the board, plus recursion depth.
Most Important Observation: validating BEFORE placing (not after filling the whole board) is what makes the search practically feasible.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known, moderately hard backtracking problem generalizing N-Queens to three constraint types.
One line memory trick: fill the next empty cell, check row/column/box first, recurse, undo on failure.
